milestones.title: Capital of Mughal Bengal
milestones.detail: Subahdar Islam Khan Chishti moved the capital of Bengal from Rajmahal to Dhaka, until then a small town and military outpost, and renamed it Jahangirnagar.

milestones.title: Bara Katra built
milestones.detail: Mir Abul Qasim, diwan of the governor Shah Shuja, built the great riverside caravanserai known as the Bara Katra.

milestones.title: Lalbagh Fort begun
milestones.detail: Prince Muhammad Azam began the Lalbagh (Aurangabad) fort during his 15 months as viceroy; his successor Shaista Khan left it unfinished.

milestones.title: Provincial government leaves for Murshidabad
milestones.detail: Murshid Quli Khan moved his seat to Murshidabad. Dhaka kept a deputy governor (Naib Nazim) but lost its court, and a long decline began.
milestones.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India (1908), vol. 11, 'Dacca City', pp. 116-119, https://archive.org/details/imperialgazettee11greauoft; Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh, 'Dhaka', https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Dhaka

milestones.title: East India Company takes full control
milestones.detail: The Company took over the remaining powers of the Naib Nazim. With the loss of its textile trade the city shrank sharply over the following decades.

milestones.title: City shrinks to under 70,000
milestones.detail: A census found 68,038 inhabitants, against an estimated 200,000 in 1800; suburbs such as Narinda and Wari had been largely abandoned.
milestones.source: Allen, Eastern Bengal District Gazetteers: Dacca (1912), https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.32851; Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh, 'Dhaka', https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Dhaka

milestones.title: Sepoy rising at Lalbagh
milestones.detail: Sepoys stationed in the fort were disarmed after a sharp fight in which 41 were killed.
milestones.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India (1908), vol. 11, 'Dacca City', pp. 116-119, https://archive.org/details/imperialgazettee11greauoft

milestones.title: Dacca Municipality established
milestones.detail: The municipality began regulating building, roads and sanitation; piped water followed in 1877.
milestones.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India (1908), vol. 11, 'Dacca City', pp. 116-119, https://archive.org/details/imperialgazettee11greauoft

milestones.title: Railway opens
milestones.detail: The Narayanganj-Dacca section of the Dacca State Railway opened on 4 January 1885, and the line to Mymensingh the following year.
milestones.source: Ahmed, Sharif Uddin (1986), Dacca: A Study in Urban History and Development, p. 99, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Dhaka

milestones.title: Tornado
milestones.detail: A tornado in April 1888 demolished 3,527 houses, damaged the Nawab's palace and killed 130 people.
milestones.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India (1908), vol. 11, 'Dacca City', pp. 116-119, https://archive.org/details/imperialgazettee11greauoft

milestones.title: Capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam
milestones.detail: Dhaka became the capital of the new province, with a lieutenant-governor, a high court and a secretariat. The province was short-lived, but the change spurred the city's growth.
milestones.source: Imperial Gazetteer of India (1908), vol. 11, 'Dacca City', pp. 116-119, https://archive.org/details/imperialgazettee11greauoft; Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh, 'Dhaka', https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Dhaka

milestones.title: University of Dhaka established
milestones.detail: The University of Dhaka was established.

milestones.title: Capital of East Bengal in Pakistan
milestones.detail: With the end of British rule Dhaka became the capital of the province of East Bengal (later East Pakistan). Migration roughly doubled its population and the urban area grew from 6 to 25 square miles by 1962.

milestones.title: Capital of independent Bangladesh
milestones.detail: The Pakistani army surrendered at the Ramna Race Course on 16 December 1971 and Dhaka became the national capital.

milestones.title: Dhaka Metro Rail opens
milestones.detail: The first section of the metro opened on 28 December 2022.

landmarks.name: Lalbagh Fort
landmarks.note: Begun in 1678 and never completed. Height is that of the inner southern fortification wall.

landmarks.name: Ahsan Manzil
landmarks.note: Built 1859-1872; damaged by the 1888 tornado and repaired. Height is the top of the dome above ground.

landmarks.name: Central Shaheed Minar
landmarks.note: Inaugurated 21 February 1963, destroyed in March 1971 and rebuilt from 1972 to a modified version of the 1963 design. Wikipedia gives the 14 m height without a citation.

landmarks.name: Baitul Mukarram National Mosque
landmarks.note: Eight-storey main building, 30.18 m above ground level.

landmarks.name: Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban (National Parliament House)
landmarks.note: Designed by Louis Kahn; opened 15 February 1982.

landmarks.name: National Martyrs' Memorial (Jatiya Smriti Saudha)
landmarks.note: 150 ft at its highest point. At Savar, north-west of the city (about 27 km in a straight line from the old centre; Wikipedia says about 35 km).

landmarks.name: City Centre
landmarks.note: CTBUH marks this height as an estimate.

landmarks.name: Swadhinata Stambha (Independence Monument)
landmarks.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swadhinata_Stambha (citing Daily Manabkantha, 11 December 2012); coordinates from OpenStreetMap way 447734739
landmarks.note: Glass tower completed in 2013 on the site of the 1971 surrender. Wikipedia says the design height was revised to 150 ft and elsewhere calls it a 50 m tower.

landmarks.name: Gulshan Tower
landmarks.source: CTBUH Skyscraper Center, https://www.skyscrapercenter.com/building/gulshan-tower/17164; position: OpenStreetMap way 371772673, https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/371772673
landmarks.note: Verification (2026-11-18): CTBUH lists a 30-floor, 125 m residential Gulshan Tower at 31 Gulshan Avenue completed in 2016, but no other source was found for it. The only building of that name and address in OpenStreetMap is a 12-level commercial block at Gulshan-2, and the building is absent from the Wikipedia list of Dhaka buildings over 100 m. Height is therefore doubtful and confidence was lowered to estimated. Coordinates moved from 23.7861, 90.4167 (about 1 km south, unsourced) to the OpenStreetMap position of Gulshan Tower, 31 Gulshan Avenue.

landmarks.name: Pinnacle
landmarks.note: Listed by CTBUH as completed in 2026; the height is CTBUH's automated estimate.

notes: Start date: 1610 is the year Islam Khan made Dhaka the Mughal capital of Bengal (the 1908 Imperial Gazetteer says about 1608). The place is older: Banglapedia describes a small pre-Mughal town around today's Babubazar that was a military outpost (thana) under Akbar, the Binat Bibi Mosque carries a date in the 1450s, and tradition takes the Dhakeshwari temple back to the 12th century. No population figure exists for that earlier town, so the timeline starts with the capital. Population before 1872 is thin and uncertain, and the series shows it: one traveller's guess for 1640, Chandler's estimates for 1700 and 1750, a disputed official estimate for 1800, counts of 1830 and 1838, and an estimate for 1867. Sources disagree widely on the Mughal peak (150,000 in Chandler; 'nearly a million' in travellers' accounts repeated by Banglapedia and Wikipedia); the lower scholarly figures are used. From 1872 the figures are censuses of the municipal area. No figure was found in the sources opened for the censuses of 1891, 1921 and 1931, and 1941 is only available rounded. There is no point at the start year. Landmarks left out for lack of a sourced height: Binat Bibi Mosque, Dhakeshwari Temple, Bara Katra and Chhota Katra, Hussaini Dalan, Sat Gambuj Mosque, Khan Mohammad Mridha Mosque (only its 16.5 ft platform is given), Star Mosque, the Armenian Church and Curzon Hall. Modern tower heights are from CTBUH, which marks City Centre and Pinnacle as estimates.
